questions.scenario: Customers complain that some transfers 'disappear': no money moved and no error shown. You find `try { ledger.post(entry); } catch (Exception e) { }` in the posting code.
questions.question: What is the right change?
options: Catch Throwable instead
Retry the post in an infinite loop
Remove the empty catch (or translate to a specific domain exception with the cause) so the failure propagates to a handler that reports it
Add e.printStackTrace() inside the catch
questions.explanation: Swallowing hides the failure from the caller, the customer and the logs. Let it propagate, or translate it into a meaningful exception that keeps the cause, and log once at the boundary.

questions.scenario: An incident report shows `LedgerException: Posting failed` with no further detail. The code was `catch (SQLException e) { throw new LedgerException("Posting failed"); }`.
questions.question: What was lost, and how do you keep it?
options: The original SQLException (and its message/stack trace); pass it as the cause: new LedgerException("Posting failed for entry " + id, e)
The return value; return null instead
Nothing was lost
The transaction; add finally
questions.explanation: Exception chaining preserves the root cause in getCause(), so logs show 'Caused by: ... duplicate key ...'. Adding the entry ID gives the investigator context.

questions.scenario: Under load the service fails with 'Connection is not available, request timed out'. Code review finds JDBC connections opened with `dataSource.getConnection()` and closed at the end of the method, but not when a query throws.
questions.question: Which construct fixes this reliably?
options: try-with-resources around the Connection, PreparedStatement and ResultSet
Call conn.close() in the catch block
Call System.gc()
Increase the pool size
questions.explanation: Every exception path leaked a connection until the pool ran dry. try-with-resources closes them in all cases, in reverse order. A bigger pool only delays the outage.

questions.scenario: A security review flags this log line: `Insufficient funds for card 5399831234567890 CVV 123, PIN attempts 2`.
questions.question: How should the exception message be written?
options: Encrypt the whole log file and keep the message
Mask the PAN (e.g. last four digits only) and never include the CVV or PIN-related secrets
Base64-encode the card number
Keep it; logs are internal
questions.explanation: Exception messages end up in logs, monitoring tools and support tickets. PCI DSS forbids storing CVVs and requires PANs to be masked. Base64 is encoding, not protection.

questions.scenario: An `ExchangeRate` object is shared by the pricing, reporting and settlement modules. A bug in reporting calls `rate.setRate(...)` and settlement starts using the wrong rate mid-batch.
questions.question: What design prevents this whole class of bug?
options: Synchronise setRate
Document that setRate must not be called
Give each module its own subclass
Make ExchangeRate immutable (final fields, no setters, validated in the constructor, or a record)
questions.explanation: If the object cannot change after construction, sharing it is safe: no module can affect another, and it is also thread-safe without locks.

questions.scenario: A method checks for a missing account like this: `try { return repo.findOrThrow(number); } catch (AccountNotFoundException e) { return createDefault(); }`. Misses happen on 40% of calls.
questions.question: What is the better design?
options: Log the exception at INFO
Catch RuntimeException instead
Return Optional<Account> from the lookup and use orElseGet(this::createDefault), since an expected miss is not exceptional
Make the exception checked
questions.explanation: Exceptions for normal control flow are slow (stack traces) and misleading. When absence is an expected outcome, model it in the return type.

questions.scenario: In review you see `if (amt.compareTo(new BigDecimal("5000000")) > 0) report(tx);` with no comment.
questions.question: What is the clean-code improvement?
options: Extract a named constant such as CTR_THRESHOLD_INDIVIDUAL and, if helpful, a comment explaining which regulation sets it
Add a comment: // compare amount
Change the number to 5e6
Move the number into a local variable called x
questions.explanation: A magic number hides the business rule. A named constant makes the intent searchable and changeable in one place; a short why-comment records its regulatory source.

questions.scenario: You are making a `Statement` class immutable. It has fields `account` (String), `period` (DateRange record) and `lines` (List<Transaction>).
questions.question: Which steps are needed?
options: Provide setters that validate input
Declare the class final and all fields private final
Validate the arguments in the constructor
Copy lines with List.copyOf in the constructor and return the unmodifiable list from the getter
questions.explanation: Final class and fields, constructor validation and defensive copying of the mutable list together make it immutable. Setters, even validating ones, make it mutable.
